ideas.working_title: Phone Stolen? Do These 5 Things NOW
ideas.hook: Your phone is gone — and your email, banking, photos, messages, and payment apps may still be signed in.
ideas.problem: A stolen unlocked or accessible phone can expose accounts, payment methods, identity data, and authentication codes.
ideas.safe_action: Locate and lock the device, secure the mobile number, protect the primary email/Apple/Google account, check financial accounts, and remotely erase only when appropriate.
ideas.source_name: Apple stolen-device response / Google lost-phone response
ideas.notes: Recommended Video #10. Recovery-first test based on strong performance of WhatsApp reclaim content.

ideas.working_title: Gmail Hacked? How to Get Your Google Account Back
ideas.hook: Your password no longer works — or you see logins and changes you did not make.
ideas.problem: A compromised Google account can expose email, saved passwords, Drive files, recovery channels, and other linked services.
ideas.safe_action: Use Google Account Recovery, review recent security events/devices, restore recovery information, change the password, and enable stronger MFA.
ideas.notes: Recommended Video #11.

ideas.working_title: Bank Account Hacked? Do This in the First 15 Minutes
ideas.hook: You see a transfer or purchase you did not make.
ideas.problem: Delay after account takeover can allow additional transactions, credential changes, or linked-account abuse.
ideas.safe_action: Contact the financial institution through an official channel immediately, lock/freeze access where available, change credentials, review linked payment methods, and document/report the fraud.
ideas.source_name: FTC what to do if you were scammed
ideas.notes: Recommended Video #12. Never promise that money can always be recovered.

ideas.working_title: Instagram Hacked? How to Take Back Your Account
ideas.hook: Your email, password, or profile information suddenly changed.
ideas.problem: A hijacked Instagram account can be used to impersonate the owner and scam followers.
ideas.safe_action: Use Instagram's official hacked-account recovery flow, secure the associated email account, reset credentials, review login activity, and warn contacts if needed.
ideas.notes: Recommended Video #13.

ideas.working_title: Your Phone Suddenly Says ‘No Service’? You May Be Under Attack
ideas.hook: Calls and texts stop working — then account-reset alerts appear.
ideas.problem: SIM-swap or port-out fraud can redirect calls and text messages, including SMS authentication codes.
ideas.safe_action: Contact the carrier immediately through a trusted channel, secure the carrier account, then protect email, banking, and other high-value accounts.
ideas.notes: Recommended Video #14; recovery angle, not only prevention.

ideas.working_title: Sent Money to a Scammer? Do This Immediately
ideas.hook: The payment is already gone — but your next move still matters.
ideas.problem: Victims may freeze or assume nothing can be done after sending money.
ideas.safe_action: Contact the bank, card issuer, wire service, payment app, or gift-card company immediately and ask whether the transaction can be reversed or stopped; then secure accounts and report the fraud.
ideas.source_name: FTC what to do if you were scammed
ideas.notes: Recommended Video #15. Phrase carefully: recovery is sometimes possible, never guaranteed.

ideas.working_title: iPhone Stolen? Lock It Before They Reach Your Money
ideas.hook: Your iPhone is gone — act before someone gets into your accounts.
ideas.problem: A stolen iPhone can expose Apple Pay, messages, email, photos, and account access if the device is not secured quickly.
ideas.safe_action: Use Find My, mark the device as lost, protect the Apple Account, contact the carrier when needed, and follow Apple's stolen-device steps.
ideas.notes: Recommended Video #16.

ideas.working_title: Facebook Hacked? Kick the Hacker Out
ideas.hook: Your password changed, strange posts appear, or friends are getting messages from you.
ideas.problem: A compromised Facebook account can be used for impersonation, marketplace scams, and attacks on contacts.
ideas.safe_action: Use Facebook's official hacked-account recovery route, secure the linked email, reset credentials, review sessions, and warn contacts.
ideas.notes: Recommended Video #17.

ideas.working_title: Wallet Stolen? Do These Things in This Order
ideas.hook: Your wallet is gone — cards, ID, and personal information may all be exposed.
ideas.problem: A stolen wallet can lead to unauthorized charges and identity theft if cards and identification remain active.
ideas.safe_action: Lock or report payment cards, contact relevant issuers, protect identity/credit as appropriate, replace identification, and monitor for misuse.
ideas.notes: Recommended Video #18.

ideas.working_title: Email Hacked? Your Password Isn’t the Only Thing to Check
ideas.hook: Changing the password is only step one.
ideas.problem: Attackers can add forwarding rules, recovery addresses, app passwords, trusted devices, or sessions that survive a simple password change.
ideas.safe_action: Reset the password, sign out unknown sessions, review recovery information, forwarding/rules and app access, then enable stronger MFA.
ideas.notes: Recommended Video #19. Can be adapted for Gmail, Outlook, Yahoo as separate platform-specific Shorts.

ideas.working_title: Card Stolen? Freeze It — Then Check These 3 Things
ideas.hook: Your debit or credit card is missing.
ideas.problem: A missing card can create unauthorized purchases and, for debit cards, direct exposure to a bank account.
ideas.safe_action: Lock/freeze or report the card immediately through the issuer, review transactions, replace the card, and follow the issuer's fraud-reporting process.
ideas.notes: Recommended Video #20.

ideas.working_title: Someone Stole Your Identity. What Do You Do First?
ideas.hook: A new account, bill, or credit inquiry appears in your name.
ideas.problem: Identity theft can expand quickly across credit, tax, benefits, phone, and financial accounts.
ideas.safe_action: Start an official recovery plan at IdentityTheft.gov, place appropriate fraud alerts or freezes, contact affected companies, preserve records, and follow the personalized recovery steps.
ideas.notes: Recommended Video #21.

ideas.working_title: Lost Your Phone and Can’t Get Your Login Code? Do This
ideas.hook: Your account still works — but your two-factor code is trapped on the missing phone.
ideas.problem: Loss of an authenticator or SMS device can lock users out of critical accounts.
ideas.safe_action: Use saved backup codes, alternate approved factors, a trusted device, or the provider's official account-recovery process; then re-enroll MFA securely.
ideas.notes: Recommended Video #22.

ideas.working_title: Phone Stolen? Here’s How to Reclaim Your WhatsApp
ideas.hook: Your phone is gone, but your WhatsApp identity is tied to your phone number.
ideas.problem: A stolen phone can leave WhatsApp accessible on the device and complicate re-registration if the SIM is also lost.
ideas.safe_action: Secure or replace the SIM/number through the carrier, re-register WhatsApp on the replacement phone, review linked devices, and enable two-step verification.
ideas.notes: Recommended Video #23. Builds on strong WhatsApp recovery performance.

ideas.working_title: Passport Lost or Stolen? Here’s What To Do
ideas.hook: Your passport is missing at home or while traveling.
ideas.problem: A lost or stolen passport creates travel disruption and identity-document risk.
ideas.safe_action: Report the passport lost/stolen through the U.S. State Department process, replace it using the correct domestic or overseas procedure, and do not travel on a passport after reporting it lost/stolen.
ideas.notes: Recommended Video #24.

ideas.working_title: You Shared the Verification Code. What Do You Do NOW?
ideas.hook: The code is already sent — now the priority is taking control back.
ideas.problem: People often learn never to share a code, but need immediate recovery instructions after they already shared it.
ideas.safe_action: Re-secure the affected account immediately using the provider's official recovery flow, revoke unknown sessions/devices, reset credentials, and protect the linked phone/email account.
ideas.source_name: FTC what to do if you were scammed
ideas.notes: Signature recovery format: prevention failed, now what?

ideas.working_title: WhatsApp Hacker Changed Your PIN. Can You Still Get Back In?
ideas.hook: You re-register your number — but WhatsApp asks for a two-step verification PIN you never set.
ideas.problem: Attackers may enable or change two-step verification, creating confusion during account recovery.
ideas.safe_action: Follow WhatsApp's official re-registration and two-step verification recovery process, secure the phone number, and remove unknown linked devices once access is restored.
ideas.notes: Advanced follow-up to Video #5; verify exact waiting-period wording against current WhatsApp support before production.

ideas.working_title: Google Hacker Changed Your Recovery Phone or Email — Now What?
ideas.hook: The recovery information no longer belongs to you.
ideas.problem: Attackers often change recovery details to make a stolen account harder to reclaim.
ideas.safe_action: Use Google's account recovery process from a familiar device/location when possible and review/restore security information after access returns.

ideas.working_title: Instagram Hacker Changed Your Email — What Can You Do?
ideas.hook: You get an email saying your Instagram email address was changed.
ideas.problem: Changing the linked email can lock the legitimate owner out and give the attacker ongoing control.
ideas.safe_action: Use Instagram's official hacked-account recovery and reversal options, then secure the associated email and enable strong authentication.

ideas.working_title: Facebook Hacker Locked You Out — Start Here
ideas.hook: Your password and contact information changed and you cannot log in.
ideas.problem: Account takeovers can cut off normal login and recovery routes.
ideas.safe_action: Start at Facebook's official hacked-account page, secure the linked email, and review active sessions and account changes after recovery.

ideas.working_title: Microsoft Account Hacked? How to Recover It
ideas.hook: Your Microsoft password changed or Outlook/Xbox activity is not yours.
ideas.problem: A compromised Microsoft account can affect Outlook email, OneDrive, Xbox, subscriptions, and Windows-linked services.
ideas.safe_action: Use Microsoft's compromised-account recovery process, review security information and sessions, reset credentials, and enable stronger authentication.

ideas.working_title: Sent Money Through a Payment App to a Scammer? Act Fast
ideas.hook: You realize the person was fake after the payment was sent.
ideas.problem: Payment-app scams can move money quickly and victims may not know whom to contact first.
ideas.safe_action: Report the fraudulent transaction to the payment app and linked bank/card immediately, ask about reversal options, secure the account, and report the scam.
ideas.source_name: FTC what to do if you were scammed
ideas.notes: Avoid guaranteeing reimbursement.

ideas.working_title: Wired Money to a Scammer? Call These People First
ideas.hook: The wire already left your account.
ideas.problem: Wire transfers can be difficult to reverse, but immediate reporting may still matter.
ideas.safe_action: Contact the wire-transfer company and sending bank immediately and ask for a recall/reversal; then secure accounts and report the fraud.
ideas.source_name: FTC what to do if you were scammed

ideas.working_title: Gave a Scammer the Gift Card Number? Do This Right Away
ideas.hook: The code has already been shared.
ideas.problem: Gift-card scammers can drain balances quickly once they have the card number and PIN.
ideas.safe_action: Contact the gift-card issuer immediately, keep the card and receipt, ask whether funds can be recovered, and report the scam.

ideas.working_title: Someone Used Your Debit Card. What Do You Do First?
ideas.hook: A charge appears that you did not make.
ideas.problem: Unauthorized debit-card use can directly affect money in a checking account and timing matters for reporting rights.
ideas.safe_action: Contact the bank immediately using an official channel, report the unauthorized transaction/card compromise, secure access, replace the card if directed, and monitor the account.
ideas.notes: Keep legal timing details exact and sourced in the description.

ideas.working_title: Car Stolen? What To Do in the First Hour
ideas.hook: Your parking space is empty and your car is gone.
ideas.problem: People may lose time searching or posting online instead of completing the steps needed for recovery and insurance.
ideas.safe_action: Confirm it was not towed, contact local law enforcement, provide vehicle details, notify the insurer, and use manufacturer tracking only in coordination with authorities when appropriate.
ideas.notes: Avoid encouraging viewers to confront or personally track thieves.

ideas.working_title: Laptop Stolen? Protect Your Accounts Before Replacing It
ideas.hook: The computer is gone, but active sessions and saved passwords may still be accessible.
ideas.problem: A stolen laptop can expose email, cloud files, browser sessions, passwords, and workplace data.
ideas.safe_action: Use available device-location/lock tools, change high-value credentials starting with primary email, revoke sessions, notify employer/IT if applicable, and report the theft.
ideas.source_name: Microsoft device security / Apple Find My

ideas.working_title: AirPods Lost? Use Find My Before You Give Up
ideas.hook: Your AirPods are missing — but they may still appear in Find My.
ideas.problem: Users may not know which location, sound, or Lost Mode features are available for their AirPods model.
ideas.safe_action: Use Apple's official Find My guidance for the specific AirPods model and avoid confronting anyone at a suspected location.

ideas.working_title: Driver’s License Stolen? Protect Your Identity Too
ideas.hook: Replacing the card is only part of the problem.
ideas.problem: A stolen driver's license contains identity information that can be combined with other stolen data for fraud.
ideas.safe_action: Report/replace the license through the issuing state, monitor for identity misuse, and use IdentityTheft.gov if fraudulent activity appears.
ideas.notes: State replacement rules vary; production should localize or keep instructions general.

ideas.working_title: Airline Lost Your Luggage? Do This Before Leaving the Airport
ideas.hook: The carousel stops — and your bag never arrives.
ideas.problem: Travelers can miss important reporting/documentation steps if they leave before creating a baggage claim record.
ideas.safe_action: Report the missing bag to the airline immediately, obtain the baggage claim/reference information, keep receipts and travel documents, and follow the airline/DOT process for delayed or lost baggage.

ideas.working_title: House Keys Stolen? Don’t Only Make a Spare
ideas.hook: If the thief can connect the keys to your address, replacing the key is not enough.
ideas.problem: Stolen keys can create ongoing home-access risk when they can be linked to the residence.
ideas.safe_action: Assess whether the keys can be tied to the address, consider rekeying/changing locks promptly, secure garage/access devices, and report related theft as appropriate.
ideas.notes: Use common-sense safety framing; avoid overstating risk.

ideas.working_title: FTC Scam Reality Check: Americans Reported $15.9 Billion Lost in 2025
ideas.hook: Three million fraud reports. $15.9 billion in reported losses. What scams caused the biggest damage?
ideas.problem: People see isolated scam stories without understanding the scale or which categories are causing the largest reported losses.
ideas.safe_action: Present the latest official FTC figures with the reporting year and publication date on screen, explain that reported losses understate total harm, and link every primary source in the description.
ideas.notes: Current official figures cited by FTC: 3 million fraud reports; $15.9B reported losses; more than 1M imposter reports / >$3.5B losses; $7.9B investment-scam losses. Re-check immediately before production.

ideas.working_title: FTC: Social-Media Scam Losses Hit $2.1 Billion in 2025
ideas.hook: Nearly 30% of people who reported losing money to a scam said it started on social media.
ideas.problem: Social-media scams are often treated as isolated messages even though FTC data show large and rapidly growing reported losses.
ideas.safe_action: Show the exact FTC numbers, explain the most common/high-loss scam categories, and direct viewers to independently verify offers and accounts.
ideas.notes: Official FTC figures: $2.1B reported losses in 2025; nearly 30% of money-loss reporters said the scam started on social media; losses about 8x 2020. Re-check before publication.

ideas.working_title: FTC: Imposter Scams Cost People $3.5 Billion in 2025
ideas.hook: Nearly one in three fraud reports involved an imposter scam.
ideas.problem: Fake bank, business, and government contacts exploit authority and urgency, but viewers may not realize how common or costly they are.
ideas.safe_action: Use the FTC's latest statistics to show the scale, then give one clear rule: independently contact the real organization using a trusted app/site/number.
ideas.notes: Official FTC figures: $3.5B reported imposter-scam losses; nearly 1 in 3 fraud reports; nearly $1B business impersonators; about $920M government impersonators. Re-check before publication.

ideas.working_title: What Are the Biggest Scams Right Now? FTC Data, Explained in 30 Seconds
ideas.hook: Instead of viral guesses, use the newest FTC Consumer Sentinel numbers.
ideas.problem: Scam trends change, while recycled social posts often quote old or unsourced statistics.
ideas.safe_action: At production time, pull the newest FTC Consumer Sentinel/Data Spotlight figures, date-stamp every statistic, compare with the prior period, and link the original FTC pages in the description.
ideas.notes: Recurring REAL-LIFE IQ format. Never call annual/periodic FTC data ‘live’ unless it is actually live; say ‘latest official FTC data as of [date].’

ideas.working_title: New FTC Scam Alert: What Changed and What You Should Do
ideas.hook: A new FTC Data Spotlight or major fraud release just dropped.
ideas.problem: Important official scam trend updates may take weeks or months to reach ordinary consumers in a usable format.
ideas.safe_action: Turn each material new FTC fraud release into a short: exact statistic, what changed, who is affected, one action to take, and primary-source links in the description.
ideas.notes: Recurring watch item; research fresh sources immediately before scripting.
